summary: Defines and registers +json-seq as a structured syntax suffix for media types built on JSON text sequences.

plainLanguage.summary: A label ending that says this file type is built on a certain kind of JSON list.

questions: how to indicate json text sequences in media types
subtitle: A media type label for files built on JSON text sequences

tldr.problem: Media types need a clear way to indicate they are built on JSON text sequences, just as existing types indicate they use plain JSON.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers '+json-seq' as a structured syntax suffix, allowing types like 'application/something+json-seq' to declare their foundation.
tldr.outcome: Applications can recognize and process any +json-seq type using generic JSON text sequence tools and can extend that generic processing with their own logic.

today: RFC 8091 is an Internet Standard Track document and remains valid. The +json-seq suffix is registered with IANA and available for use in new media types.

sections.title: What is a Media Type Suffix
sections.content: Media types (also called MIME types, like 'application/json' or 'text/html') describe what kind of data is in a file or message. Structured syntax suffixes are short labels added to the end of a media type to signal what the file is built on top of. They follow the pattern 'type/name+suffix'. For example, the '+json' suffix says 'this type is built on JSON.' RFC 8091 introduces '+json-seq' for files built on JSON text sequences, which are multiple JSON objects separated by special characters.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like putting a sticker on a box that says 'made from wood' or 'contains plastic.' The sticker tells you what the basic building block is.

sections.title: JSON Text Sequences
sections.content: A JSON text sequence is a standard way to send multiple JSON values in a single stream. Instead of putting them all in one array (like '[1, 2, 3]'), you send each JSON value separately, separated by record separators and line feeds. This matters for systems that process data in real time or in very large batches, because you can start reading and handling values as they arrive, rather than waiting for the entire file. The format is defined in RFC 7464.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one big list, you send small individual chunks, one after another. Your program can start reading chunks right away instead of waiting for everything.

sections.title: The +json-seq Suffix
sections.content: RFC 8091 formally registers '+json-seq' as a suffix with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). Any new media type that builds on JSON text sequences can now use this suffix to say so. For example, a hypothetical type could be 'application/myformat+json-seq'. Applications that support generic JSON text sequence processing can recognize the suffix and use their standard tools. Type-specific applications can layer custom behavior on top of that generic processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Now anyone who invents a new file type can put '+json-seq' at the end of its name, and all programs will know it is made from JSON text sequences.
